title: Ἀλώπηξ πρὸς μορμολύκειον
part: The Fox and the Mask (Chambry 43 · Perry 27)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 43 (= Perry 27). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ εἰς οἰκίαν ἐλθοῦσα ὑποκριτοῦ καὶ ἕκαστα τῶν αὐτοῦ σκευῶν διερευνωμένη, εὗρε καὶ κεφαλὴν μορμολυκείου εὐφυῶς κατεσκευασμένην, ἣν καὶ ἀναλαβοῦσα ταῖς χερσὶν ἔφη· « Ὦ οἵα κεφαλή, καὶ ἐγκέφαλον οὐκ ἔχει. »
sentences.tr: Alōpēx eis oikian elthousa hypokritou kai hekasta tōn autou skeuōn diereunōmenē, heure kai kephalēn mormolykeiou euphyōs kateskeuasmenēn, hēn kai analabousa tais chersin ephē· « Ō hoia kephalē, kai enkephalon ouk echei. »
sentences.l: A fox, having-come into the house of an actor and searching-through each of his properties, found also a bogey's head, skilfully fashioned, which, having-taken-up in her hands, she said: « O what a head, and it has no brain. »
sentences.i: A fox came into an actor's house, and as she rummaged through each piece of his gear she found a bogey's head, skilfully made. She took it up in her hands and said: « What a head — and no brain in it! »
sentences.n: A μορμολύκειον is the bogey used to frighten children, and so the grotesque mask that represents it on the stage; the fox is going through an actor's σκεύη, his props. εὐφυῶς is 'skilfully, deftly' — the mask is well made, which is the whole joke. Ὦ οἵα κεφαλή is exclamatory, 'what a head!', and the point turns on ἐγκέφαλος, literally 'the in-the-head thing', the brain. Greek gives the fox χεῖρες, 'hands', without apology.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος πρὸς ἄνδρας μεγαλοπρεπεῖς μὲν τῷ σώματι, κατὰ ψυχὴν δὲ ἀλογίστους.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos pros andras megaloprepeis men tōi sōmati, kata psychēn de alogistous.
sentences.l: The fable is directed at men magnificent indeed in body, but in soul without judgment.
sentences.n: A closing tag with no verb: πρός with the accusative marks the sort of person the fable is aimed at, and the 'is' is left to be understood. μέν … δέ sets the two halves against each other — τῷ σώματι, a dative of respect, against κατὰ ψυχήν.
